title: The Top Score
dateline: Selrick Academy. The first entrance assessment.
mood: One needle, one year of split knuckles, and a seat in the stand that stays empty.

hero.alt: Chang'e, small, in round glasses and a white coat, holds a pen and a board in a doorway; Lesley stands behind her in a white officer's coat, her blonde hair falling over one eye.

segs.t: Inside the gate, a queue of about a hundred children ran the length of the yard. Guinevere stood near the back, her cold hands in her pockets.

At the front stood a table with a glove on it, wired to a dial that read aspirant power. Behind it, on a stool, sat a girl smaller than anyone in the queue, in a white coat cut to her size. A round white robot with long ears floated at her shoulder.
The examiner is younger than me,
thought Guinevere.
At the wall behind the table stood a young woman with a long rifle on her back and a dark visor over one eye. She watched the queue and left the dial to the girl.
Each child put a hand in the glove. It hummed and lit, and the needle swung. Some snatched their hands back at the hum. One boy ran back toward the gate. The woman with the rifle watched him go.

Far ahead, a girl with pink-red twin-tails put her hand in the glove. Word came back down the queue: her needle had hit the stop. She walked on to the far door and never once looked back to see who was behind her.

A needle past the line meant that door, and the Combat Division’s preparatory course: a year of training before any real fight. The rest went left, to the Support Division, to learn to mend Aspirants and their suits.

blocks.caption: A Combat Division trainee, and the Support Division’s long coat.

segs.t: The queue moved. Now the black-haired girl from the gate stood just ahead. Her cloth bag clinked when she set it down.
“Hand in the glove,” said the small girl, fast, as if she had said it all morning. “I’m Chang’e. I read the needle. Lesley asks the questions.”
The needle passed the line.
“Name,” said Lesley.
“Vexana.”
“Why are you here?”
“To destroy the Enders.”
Lesley looked at her a long moment, then tipped her head at the far door. Vexana took her bag and went.
Guinevere stepped up. The glove was still warm inside. It hummed. She did not pull back. The needle swung past the line and stayed there.
“Name.”
“Guinevere of House Baroque.”
Behind her the queue murmured. She heard the word
Baroque
twice.
“Why are you here?”
“To become the top Aspirant.”
Chang’e looked up from the dial. “The top of what?”
“All of it.”
Lesley’s face did not change. “Next.”
Guinevere walked to the far door and did not hurry.
Nobody can buy a needle,
she thought.
That one was mine.
The preparatory year.

In her first week she stopped at the fountain in the courtyard. On the wall above it hung a brass plaque: WITH THANKS TO THE PATRONS OF SELRICK ACADEMY. Under it were the families who gave the Academy money. HOUSE BAROQUE came first.

media.alt: Two cadets in dark uniforms walk across the courtyard toward the Academy's tall white main building under a clear blue sky.
media.credit: Official interactive drama, Guinevere and Vexana

segs.t: He paid for this too,
she thought.
And never said.
Behind her, two cadets were filling their flasks.
“Baroque money,” said one.
“She didn’t need the glove,” said the other. “Her father paid for it.”
Guinevere turned and gave them her widest smile. They went red and left.
The course ends with a trial,
she thought.
I’ll take the top score. And they’ll all have to see.

In her third week the sirens went for real. Enders were loose in a far ward. The instructors herded the cadets into a concrete shelter with slits for windows. One of them stood in the door. “Inside. Nobody leaves.”
Everyone crowded to the slits, Guinevere too. Then she looked around.
Vexana sat alone on the bench by the door. Her hands lay flat on her knees. She did not move. Her eyes stayed on the door.
Doesn’t she want to see?
thought Guinevere.
When the all-clear sounded, Vexana was the last one out.
At dawn Guinevere ran the grounds and hit the heavy bag bare-fisted, the way Hester had taught her. Only then did she call up her two new drones.
They ran on her aspirant power. Holding both up at once was the hardest thing she had ever learned. When her power ran low, their yellow rings dimmed and they sagged.
One morning both of them dropped at once, onto her feet.
“Ow,” said Guinevere, hopping. “Ow.” She glared down at them. “That was not elegant.”
She picked them up and called them again.

Her knuckles split, and she taped them. She carried band-aids in every pocket, for herself and for anyone else. When a boy in her drill line skinned his palm, she had one on it before he could say no.
“Baroque money,” she told him. “It paid for this too.”
He stared at it and laughed, and so did she.
Each week she mailed home every sum her House tutors set, so he could not say she had let them slip. She wrote
Father,
at the top of every letter. In the first one, under the last sum, she added a line.
I can hold two drones now. Nearly.
On rest days she asked at the gate for post.
“Nothing today,” said the guard.
At night, after the last cadet had gone, she came back to the training hall. She lit only the lamp that hung on a chain over the heavy bag.
One night her drones began to sag after an hour. She held them up anyway, her arms shaking, until their rings came back a shade. Under her breath she said, “With this power, stronger still.”
High above the door, in the gallery where the lamp never reached, Vexana lowered her practice staff.
She trained up there every night without a sound. In the day she ate alone and answered in one word.
Below, the heiress was talking to her drones again. Bare fists first, then the drones. It was always that order.
She has a long car and a woman who calls her miss,
thought Vexana.
What is she doing in here at midnight?
Vexana set her feet and raised the staff. Under her breath she said, “Strengthen this resolve even further.”
When her forms were done, she went down the stair and out. Under the lamp, the heiress never looked up.
The last weeks of the preparatory course.
Its final combat trial was scored by the instructors. It never went on the rankings board. It decided nothing but pride.
Under her last page of sums, Guinevere added a line.
The final trial is in ten days. Please come and watch.
Four days before the trial, a guard called her to the gate. Hester stood outside the bars in her gray coat.
“Your father has a board meeting, miss.”
It was the first answer all year.
“Oh,” said Guinevere. She held on to one of the bars. “Will you come?”
“I have the House’s pass, miss.”
In the stand on the training field, the patrons had the front row. A card on one seat said HOUSE BAROQUE. The seat was empty.
Two rows behind it sat Hester, upright, her hands in her lap.
Board meetings end,
thought Guinevere.
He could still come late.
Steel dummies built like Enders ran at the cadets on rails, one cadet at a time. When a dummy swung, its chest plates opened, as a real Ender’s did. Three instructors marked score sheets at a table.
When her name was called, Guinevere looked at the empty seat. Then she walked out with both drones up.

She did not wait for the first dummy to reach her. It swung, and she went under its arm and put her fist into its open chest. A drone cracked the next one across the head and turned it for her. She hit it before it finished turning.
Halfway through, the drones dipped. She did not look at them.
I’ve dropped you on my feet all year,
she thought.
Not today.
She hit the next dummy harder, and the drones came up with her.
When the last dummy stopped on its rail, the stand clapped. Hester did not.

The other cadets ran. Late in the day the instructors signed their sheets and called Guinevere back. One of them gave her a beginner’s medal on a ribbon and one sheet of paper under the Academy’s crest. At the bottom, in red ink beside three sets of initials, were two words.
Top score.
She looked up at the front row. The card still sat on the empty seat. Two rows behind it, Hester was clapping, alone in her row.
I’ll take it to him myself,
thought Guinevere.
She folded the paper once and slid it inside her jacket, over her heart.
